WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

THE WHOLE CEP IN ONE SENTENCE

“How hard can we test the app before we spend our allowance for failures?”

The controller is the person watching the allowance. Attribution is checking which failures the test actually caused. The watchdog is a separate person who stops the drill if the controller disappears.

Four modules, one feedback loop

→→→

The first three inform the live loop. The oracle summarizes completed runs; it does not predict the future.

Where the real tools fit

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

What this visualizer simplifies

It samples synthetic requests using a fixed seed, with no shared infrastructure, retries, or delayed telemetry. Intentional delays are 600ms; requests over 500ms or failed requests count against the latency SLO. Healthy responses have no extra random latency.

The allocation is frozen at admission from a declared 120-second reservation, even when traffic changes. We do not observe that entire horizon. The loop uses instantaneous synthetic observations; its reserve does not simulate real cleanup damage. Known background failures cancel only approximately because cohorts have different random samples.

The normal teaching mode charges the nonnegative point estimate of extra failures. Repository v2 modes port the current realized-cumulative-v2 accounting: cumulative observed treatment bad events, a never-refunded high-water mark, and (optionally) a background credit that is valid only under declared iid assumptions. The retired v1 mode is kept only to show the old per-interval Wilson error. None of these modes validates the real controller, proves causality, or establishes a strict budget bound.

Read these results carefully

These are 60-second teaching simulations using one seed, not the CEP's final empirical evaluation. The preplanned policy uses an illustrative cost of one bad request per affected request. It has not been calibrated on cluster pilots. Adaptive behavior is inspired by the prototype; time windows and real actuator delays are simplified.

All policies share an emergency allocation guard. Similar overshoot can mean the shared guard dominated the comparison. No winner is claimed from this demonstration.

Evidence at a glance

Headline findings, with their limits

    Policy means by fault family and load

    Mean over replication blocks (n=5 each). Latency SLO. Exposure is in .

    Adaptive controller versus each comparator

    Paired difference = closed-loop minus comparator, latency SLO, mean with descriptive 95% bootstrap interval over five blocks. Negative overshoot means less.

    Follow-up: spending the budget on purpose

    In the main study the adaptive controller used only about 30% of the usable abort allowance. Its safety gates (burn rate) throttled it, not its budget. After seeing those results we added a policy and ran : further runs. It was chosen after the main results, was collected about a week later, and is paired with the main study by block ID only. It is never pooled with it, and a jointly randomized study is still needed.

    Differences are paced minus the earlier policy (fraction-seconds), with 95% block-bootstrap intervals, from results/curated/followup-table.tex. Text summary from docs/DECISIONS.md: paced spent 98–100% of the usable allocation, but nine of 20 runs overshot the usable guard by 1–4 requests and seven were ended by the allocation safety guard; no run exceeded its allocation.

    What went wrong, and was kept

    One attempt failed when the host suspended on 8 November. Stale telemetry triggered the stop; the watchdog removed the fault and the API confirmed it was gone, but draining timed out. The attempt stayed failed (a ) and its single predeclared retry completed. No valid unfavorable result was retried, and all attempts are archived as .
